ai_show_review.summary: Red‑hot second set w/ Alligator>Caution saga & monster New Potato
ai_show_review.blurb: The February 14 1968 show delivers a blistering second set highlighted by the Alligator → Caution → Feedback sequence, a soaring New Potato Caboose, and an incendiary Spanish Jam. Jerry’s guitar is crisp and monster‑level while Pigpen’s organ dominates the improvisations. The overall performance ranks among the band’s early‑‘68 peaks.
ai_show_review.review: On Valentine's Day 1968 at San Francisco’s Carousel Ballroom the Dead unleashed a high‑octane set that still feels fresh decades later. After a tight first set capped by Dark Star → China Cat Sunflower → The Eleven, the band dove into an epic second set that mirrors the Anthem of the Sun album: Cryptical Envelopment segues into The Other One, then back into another Cryptical before launching into New Potato Caboose and Born Cross‑Eyed. From there the group erupts into a Spanish Jam that rolls straight into the legendary Alligator → Caution (Do Not Stop On Tracks) → Feedback chain, capped with an encore of In The Midnight Hour. Jerry’s “fat crunchy” tone is crisp yet ferocious, delivering monster solos that sound almost composed on the fly. Phil’s bass takes on a lead‑guitar quality, driving the Eleven and locking in tight with Mickey and Bill’s eight‑limbed drum machine. Pigpen’s calliope organ is front‑and‑center, providing the backbone for Dark Star, Alligator and the Spanish Jam, while his vocals add an extra layer of raw energy. The recording quality varies—from fair FM captures to crystal‑clear soundboards—but even the roughest sources convey the show’s relentless intensity, making this night a must‑listen for any Deadhead seeking early‑‘68 fire.

best_recording.reason: Widely cited as the definitive source for the red‑hot second set despite uncertain source, it captures the full flow of the legendary jams.

key_highlights: Alligator → Caution → Feedback sequence erupts with relentless drive.
New Potato Caboose launches a soaring jam that segues flawlessly into Born Cross‑Eyed.
Spanish Jam showcases Pigpen’s organ dominance and the band’s improvisational peak.
Dedication to Neal Cassady in the second set adds historic poignancy.

band_performance.Jerry: Garcia’s guitar is crisp and “fat crunchy,” delivering monster‑level solos that feel like mini‑compositions; his stage presence is described as captivating and “wow fucking cool.”
band_performance.Phil: Lesh’s bass adopts a manic lead‑guitar style, driving The Eleven and underpinning the jams with solid, propulsive lines despite occasional flat tuning.
band_performance.Bob: Weir’s rhythm guitar evolves into a monster foundation, providing strong vocals for the era and locking tightly into the improvisations.
band_performance.Mickey: Hart (and Bill) form a symbiotic eight‑limbed rhythm machine that powers the set with propulsive grooves.
band_performance.Billy: Kreutzmann’s drumming meshes seamlessly with Hart, delivering tight, energetic support throughout the jams.
